Heuristics for bit, cryptarithm and equations — NVIDIA Nemotron Model Reasoning Challenge


NVIDIA Nemotron Model Reasoning Challenge
Solution Writeup · 109th place · Jun 16, 2026

I've accidentialy found this competition in a few weeks before the deadline. As most of us I tried
to improve awesome baseline solution by @huikang. Unfortunately, I didn't have enough time to
make my CoTs short enough, so only one small change actually moved me up in leaderboard.
But I want to share some thoughts and ideas I came up.

Bit manipulation
tldr; found set of 3 parameters functions that covers all cases. Search for two-parameter
functions matches and filter them out looking at bits 0 and 7 of the output and searching where
input bits 7 and 0 are involved.

If you read definition of the task it is clearly states:

        The transformation involves operations like bit shifts, rotations, XOR, AND, OR,
        NOT, and possibly majority or choice functions

So, I've decided to search for this 3 argument functions. AND-3 appeared to be useless, it's cases
are fully covered by Majority.

My final investigator finds solution for each of 1602 tasks (match any). And potentially reasoner
could solve up to 1577 tasks using only this basis:

    •   XOR: 625
    •   MAJ: 459
    •   XOR_OR: 234
    •   OR: 148
    •   OR_XNOR: 58
    •   CHOICE: 53

I've also changed a list of transformations to achieve it. All negation operations should be
applied before transformations. Instead of Not(Shift(x)), I use Shift(Not(x)), etc.
Shrinking possible arguments combinations to Rot(1-7), and two Shift(1-7) in any direction still
giving 1522 correct answers.
If we add combination like Rot + Rot + Shift, but only for Xor operator - it gives 1576.
But we still can't just brute-force all possible combinations. Here comes in some additional
heuristics. Basically there only three cases:




As you can see, in all cases we have some space, where it is guaranteed to have only one- or two-
parameters function. So we can use the original @huikangs approach to find such spots and try
to build them one line. I've made a bit broader covering to handle negated operands correctly.

To compress the CoT for additional operators I build also negated-output matching table. It gives
e.g. if one of AND candidates matched to the negative one, then it is by the De Morgan's low
Not(A and B) -> Not(A) or Not(B)

After that we have a few groups:

g_xor = XOR, XOR-NOT
g_or = OR, OR-NOT, NOT-OR, NOT-OR-NOT
g_and = AND, AND-NOT, NOT-AND, NOT-AND-NOT
g_iden = Identity, NOT
content_copy

1) Two left-shifts or two right-shifts

In this case we check what happens on side and what is in the middle.

 Side Middle     Candidate function
g_iden gxor XOR3, OR_XNOR, XOR_OR
g_iden g_or OR3, XOR_OR
g_iden g_and OR_XNOR, CHOICE
g_iden g_iden CHOICE
 Side Middle    Candidate function
C0    g_and MAJ

After that we have a lot of candidates and we try to filter-out as much as possible before final
brute-force. There are two branches: LShift and RShift but they are quite symmetric.

Lets take a look at LShift+LShift+Rot case in the picture:




We will have at least one identity match on the right side.
Using the Identity candidate (index 2 in this case), we can calculate rotation LRot(3) and find the
first spot spot to the left, where two parameter function matches. We are looking only for
candidates who has 7 as one of indexes (0 for right shift) and match selected rotation in the same
position.
If it is not found - we check the next one. In this picture the perfect candidate would have match
to 7-7 and three Identity matches in a row to the right of it.

Now we have a few pairs of ROT(const)+LShift(const)+LShift(x) - the last one we can just
brute-force. But as heuristic we can use the fact, that we must see some amount of two operands
operations matches in a row. So as the first candidate we should use the spot where it ends (in
picture 7-6-6).

My problem was here mostly with C0 candidates or AND operations, because they give too
much candidates when the output columns are like "000000"

2,3 Left shift + Right shift

This case is easier. You guaranted to see on the both sides some matches. In most cases you can
easily calculate the Rotation candidate.
In case (2) a good pair from both sides selected, where on of indexes is X for the left side and X-1
mod 8 for the right.
E.g. AND33, XOR26 -> LRot(3), LShift(3), RShift(1).
Then we calculate where they should overlap and check if the sequence for each function
continues till that point:




For left-right I also have a table of candidate functions, but now they are divided by sides:

 Left Rght Candidate function
g_xor g_xor XOR3, OR_XNOR
g_or g_or OR3, XOR_OR
g_and g_and MAJ, CHOICE
 Left Rght Candidate function
g_xor g_or XOR_OR
g_and g_xor OR_XNOR
g_and g_iden CHOICE
g_and C0     Maj

For the case (3) we can also check the middle for Identity/Constant matches that should be in
between of shifts.

2 Rotation + Shift




Additional ~50 tasks could be solved if we check such cases with XOR function. And it is quite
easy to do actually. Lets take a look at XOR-3 ANF:

XOR(A,B,C) = A ⊕ B ⊕ C; then XOR(A,B,C) ⊕ C = A ⊕ B ⊕ C ⊕ C = A ⊕ B

We have a list of all possible XOR(A,B) and Output is XOR(A,B,C). The only thing we have to
do is to build list of possible XOR(Output, C) and match it on the XOR(A,B) table.

Why it all didn't work

My mistake was, that I've spend too much time trying to reach a perfect solution. I could apply
e.g. only the XOR3 heuristic, it would already give me some small boost..
I've implemented everything above, but there were a lot of cases where final brute-force is too
big and I didn't have enough time how to compress it. I think the good enough solution would be
to score each potential candidate by length and how much info does it gives. Most of bad cases
were output columns with 00000 or 111111.

Another approach

I also had another approach in mind that I didn't have time to try. It is the same trick as for XOR
function. We can write down ANFs for all functions, partially calculate them and then XOR it on
the output:

OR(x,y,z)=x⊕y⊕z⊕xy⊕xz⊕yz⊕xyz

XOR_OR(x,y,z)=x⊕y⊕z⊕xz⊕yz
Choice(x,y,z)=z⊕xy⊕xz

Maj(x,y,z)=xy⊕xz⊕yz

XOR(x,y,z)=x⊕y⊕z

OR_XNOR(x,y,z)=1⊕x⊕y⊕z⊕xy

The xyz is a bit problematic, but it could be resolved for only appropriate candidates on the
edges. Same approach - we make XOR on Output and match on one of pre-calculated tables. I
think this one was really perspective…

Cryptarythm
For cryptarythm it was important to understand the restrictions of the dataset itself. It is possible
to correctly determine the right class of operators in 781 cases out of 823 in total if restrict the
operations by following classes:

Concatenation -> concat, reverse concat, big\little-endian

Multiplication -> mul + offset{-1,0,1}

Summation -> sum + offset{-1,0,1}

Substraction -> absdiff, signed substraction, negative absdiff, right-left substraction

How to map them? In most cases the meaning is the same as symbols semantic. Like * is mul, +
is sum, etc.
But sometime we don't have appropriate symbols. And also sometimes the original symbols
change meaning. We can check such cases by simple rules:

   •   check for concats first (+ and * are also quite often concats)
   •   If we don't have *,-,+ we look at right side size (4 -> mul, 1 -> sub, 2-> sum\sub, 3 ->
       sum\mul).
   •   for *,-,+ apply by their meaning if there are no contradictions
   •   If some of the operations are taken, then use another one for yours
   •   if operator is only in question (guess tasks) - use unused operation. If there multiple - use
       opposite to the presented one. E.g. * is substraction from exaples, then / in question is
       summation, etc.

This list is not full, but you got the idea - even for the guess questions there are some deduction
steps how to find good candidate for the operation.
Full determenistic search gives 751 right answers in such constraints.

After that I build mappings and write down equations with offsets and substraction branching
included for big and little endian. Something like this:
Big-endian mapped formulas:
E1: 10*A+B+10*C+D+m=100*E+10*C+E # m is offset for multiplication
E2: (10*F+E)*(10*B+D)+l=1000*E+100*A+10*D+D # l is offset for summation
E3: 10*G+D+10*G+H+m=100*E+10*I+I
content_copy

After that I build mod 10 restrictions. It cut many branches early:

Big-endian mod 10 constraints:
Use full equations modulo 10 before decimal columns.
M1: B+D+m=1 (mod 10)
M2: D+l=D (mod 10)
M3: D+H+m=I (mod 10)
Combined mod 10 propagation:
  P1: l in {0}
content_copy

Then I make equtaions for units, tens, hundreds etc for summation and substraction only. It
creates carries, which easy to iterate through.

E3: GD+GH+m=1II
  E3.C1 units: D+H+m=I+10*c3
  E3.D1: c3 in {-1,0,1}
  E3.C2 tens: G+G+c3=I+10*c4
  E3.D2: c4 in {-1,0,1}
  E3.C3 hundreds: c4=1
content_copy

And then just brute-force, selecting on each step the smallest set for branching, checking
constraints and building local ones for branch.
When there are small enough search field ( < 5000 combinations) I add mod 37 to cut some
branches quicker.
Also, mod 11 is helpful for polyndrom numbers like HH, FIIF, etc And mod 100 for
multiplication.
I also stop after 13k symbols to keep it shorter then 7k tokens.

I solved this way 391 tasks. But I finished this solution just before the deadline, and didn't have
time to setup training correctly. It gave me 0,82 result with all other classic samples =\ I think
overfitting took place here…

Equations (guess)
I gained like +50 tasks in equations category. I think it is the only reason why I moved from
1000+ place to 115 in the end :)



The idea for sign is the same as for cryptarythms:
    •    if arithmetic sign, use its meaning
    •    if opposite sign found in samples, use opposite meaning: e.g [ is substraction, then ] is
         addition
    •    if all other operations "taken", use unused one
         ….
    •    use default fallback

So that's it :)

That was really fun to try to solve such puzzles! Thanks everybody for the competition!
